Stan requires initial values to provide initial values for all
parameters --- you haven't specified an initial value for er.

You can either add some inits for the variable er or just
let Stan do a random initialization. Stan's good at
converging from diffuse starting points.

What is the question? You just need to specify the seed to the call to stan().
If you want to reproduce R's behavior, you need to set the R seed (and make sure
any global variables in your scripts are the same before starting).

> 2. In section 23.3 of the manual "See Section 23.3.1 for a full explanation." is missing. As I need to know and
> understand more on Increment log probability for poisson_log(n,lambda).

I found two references to 23.3.1, which doesn't appear under
that number because the subsections aren't numbered. I need
to change those references to names --- 23.3.1 is just the
first subsection of section 23.3. I added a to-do item to
our manual update issue:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/325
> 3. Saving coda files for later use.

RStan doesn't read or write Coda files.

Stan's sampler does produce a stanfit object, from which samples
can be extracted. The samples can also be converted to
a data frame or matrix. The stanfit object can also be saved (without the
executable model) using the save() function in R and read
back in later with load().

If you're trying to compare Stan to BUGS or JAGS, note that the
effective sample size calcs are more conservative in Stan and that
you should only worry about number of effective samples per second.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Initial values / proper placement of 'random component' for Hierarchical PG model
parts:
The dimensionality of all parameters is defined
in terms of the data in Stan. You have N defined,
so you know the size of er. You can initialize them
all to 0 with

er = rep(0,N)

Have you tried letting Stan do random inits? The only
time it's worth doing them yourself is if there's a
computational issue with convergence using random inits
(and that often signals other problems in the model).

- Bob
